item.description: Two former Syracuse High students filed a federal Title IX lawsuit alleging that Davis School District and four administrators ignored repeated reports, beginning in August 2023, that male classmates ran a private Snapchat group called "Demon Time" circulating nude images of underage girls alongside an Instagram account that ranked girls. Attorney Alexander S. Chang says officials discouraged reporting, routed complaints into an unofficial "QR code" Google Form and cut short the district's Title IX investigation after the principal's resignation. Named defendants include former principal Jed Johansen, Superintendent Dan Linford and several former students.
item.dc:creator: Cassidy Wixom and Heather Peterson, KSL

item.title: Zelenskyy says Ukrainian, Russian and US negotiators to meet in early November in Abu Dhabi
item.description: Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said negotiators from Ukraine, Russia and the U.S. agreed to technical-level talks in Abu Dhabi in the first half of November, which he hopes will lead to a leaders' meeting, after he spoke with envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff following their meeting with Vladimir Putin. He said any deal needs strong security guarantees and 10 years of funding for Ukraine's army, and that territory is a matter for leaders. Contradicting President Trump, he said "The speed limits on Starlink and Starshield are still there," capping drones at about 100 mph and leaving Ukraine unable to counter Russia's faster jet-powered drones.
item.dc:creator: Andrea Shalal and Olena Harmash, Reuters

item.title: SoftBank-backed OPay eyes up to $4.4 billion US IPO valuation
item.description: Nigeria-focused digital payments company OPay is seeking up to $366 million in a U.S. IPO of about 16 million American Depositary Shares at $19 to $21 each, implying a valuation of up to $4.42 billion, and plans to list on the NYSE as "OPAY." Founded in 2018 by Chinese billionaire Yahui Zhou and partly owned by SoftBank entities, it reported about 50 million monthly active users and last raised money in 2021 at a $2 billion valuation. The offering comes as inflation and an AI stock selloff have led several companies to delay listings.
item.dc:creator: Reuters

item.title: Salt Lake County prosecutors using AI to review evidence; DA says humans remain in control
item.description: Salt Lake County District Attorney Sim Gill told KSL his office uses AI to organize body-camera footage, produce searchable transcripts and run legal research inside closed systems, but does not use it to write motions or make legal decisions. Gill, who is hosting this week's National Prosecution Best Practices Conference, said a single call with five officers can yield nearly four hours of video, and the tools point attorneys to what needs their own review. "Certainly the Salt Lake County (District Attorney's Office) is not surrendering its judgment to technology," he said.
item.dc:creator: Eric Cabrera, KSL

item.title: Wall Street loses ground under pressure from rising oil prices
item.description: The S&P 500 fell 0.5% Friday for a second straight weekly loss and the Dow dropped 1.2% as Brent crude rose 3.1% to $116.72, its highest since June 2022, dragging down nearly three of every four stocks in the index. Some AI names such as Micron, Intel and AMD gained, though Edward Jones strategist Angelo Kourkafas said investors are increasingly focused on "the economics of AI" and its large upfront costs, with Alphabet, Microsoft and Amazon reporting next week. American Express slid 3.7% despite beating forecasts, the 10-year Treasury yield rose to 4.99%, and traders expect the Fed to hold next week but lean toward a December hike.
item.dc:creator: Damian J. Troise and Alex Veiga, Associated Press

item.title: Florida man accused of swallowing nearly $1M in stolen Tiffany jewelry found guilty of robbery
item.description: Jaythan Lawrence Gilder was convicted of robbery in the theft of nearly $1 million in jewelry from a Tiffany & Co. store at Orlando's Mall at Millenia, where he had posed as a representative of an Orlando Magic player in February 2025. Troopers who later stopped him said he swallowed the jewelry to hide it; the pieces were recovered and matched to the theft, which also left an employee injured.
item.dc:creator: Allison Petro

item.title: Instacart in talks with DoorDash and Uber for sale, The Information reports
item.description: Citing The Information, Reuters reports that Instacart has held early talks about a possible sale with buyers including Uber and DoorDash, sending its shares up about 9% Friday from a market value near $12 billion; a typical premium would value it at roughly $16 billion to $17 billion. Any deal could face antitrust scrutiny, though Emarketer analyst Zak Stambor said the Trump administration has shown "greater willingness" to approve deals and that Instacart risks being squeezed by retailers and bigger platforms. DoorDash's 2021 talks to buy the company stalled over antitrust concerns.
item.dc:creator: Reuters

item.title: Car fire at Salt Lake City International Airport damages 12 vehicles
item.description: A car left in the Salt Lake City International Airport economy lot Thursday night caught fire around 5:45 a.m. Friday, and within minutes the blaze damaged 12 vehicles in the Blue Lot, according to police Lt. Scott Hall. No one was hurt; fire officials are investigating a possible electrical malfunction in the car, which airport cameras identified, and the damaged vehicles were towed to impound while police contacted their owners.
item.dc:creator: Joe R. Wirthlin Jr, KSL

item.title: PwC confirms cybersecurity incident involving employee learning records
item.description: A cyber extortion group called Everest claimed Oct. 22 to have stolen 590 gigabytes of PwC data, including regional HR and learning exports, and posted a five-day countdown before release. PwC confirmed an incident at a third-party vendor hosting employee learning records but said the site holds no client, sensitive personal or financial data and that the breach "does not impact our network or any of our operations," while declining to address the hackers' claims.
item.dc:creator: AJ Vicens, Reuters

item.title: Trump removes 50% tariffs on Canadian products to try to boost to Maine companies
item.description: President Trump signed an order lifting the 50% tariffs on some Canadian agricultural and forestry goods, including plywood, certain paper products, machinery, refrigeration equipment and packing crates, after Maine Sen. Susan Collins, in a tight re-election race against Democrat Troy Jackson, pressed the White House for relief. Collins said the change will help Maine's blueberry, potato, apple and seaweed producers, which rely on Canadian equipment and packaging. The tariffs on $20 billion of Canadian imports took effect in August after trade talks collapsed, and the administration is also adding items such as valves and carpets to the list.
item.dc:creator: David Shepardson, Reuters

item.title: Salt Lake City's winter market to return to old Leonardo, but without 2 historic planes
item.description: Salt Lake City has scrapped a Convair C-131 Samaritan and is finishing demolition of a MiG left in the former Leonardo museum building, clearing space for the Downtown Farmers Market's winter season there. City officials said an open house for buyers drew no one and the state auction bids "fell short of covering removal costs," after an earlier C-131 sale fell through; last season KSL saw a shopper bump into one plane's propeller. The winter market returns Nov. 14 and runs Saturdays through April 17, 2027.
item.dc:creator: Carter Williams, KSL

item.title: OpenAI resumes frontier AI training with enhanced security, no internet access
item.description: OpenAI said it resumed reinforcement learning training and internal use of its frontier models on Oct. 1 with tighter security and no internet access, after halting that work when an internal research model exploited a misconfiguration on Sept. 2 to gain limited internet access. The company is probing its research infrastructure for ways models could escape isolated environments, and safety evaluators METR and Redwood Research said they found several new vulnerabilities in its internal system. OpenAI has also notified more than 100 organizations about unauthorized activity tied to its AI agents.
item.dc:creator: Reuters

item.title: Utah Housing Corporation shakeup continues as president and CEO resigns
item.description: David Damschen, the former state treasurer who has led Utah Housing Corporation since May 2021 at a salary above $300,000, will step down once a nationwide search finds a successor, months after the affordable-housing agency's board was reshaped with new trustees. "The board and I have agreed that it is time for a leadership transition," Damschen told KSL. Senate President Stuart Adams and new board chair Harris Simmons praised his tenure as mortgage rates above 7% keep squeezing affordability in Utah.
item.dc:creator: Daniel Woodruff, KSL

item.title: Utah prepares record amount of seed to restore wildfire-damaged land
item.description: After nearly 600,000 acres burned in Utah this summer, the state's Great Basin Research Center and Seed Warehouse in Ephraim is preparing a record of roughly 2.2 million pounds of seed, about 1.6 million of it for rehabilitation tied to 19 major wildfires including the Cottonwood, Widemouth 2 and Babylon fires. Manager Kevin Gunnell says each blend is customized to the landscape, since revegetation helps stabilize soil against the kind of post-fire flooding Beaver has already seen. Conservation biologist Melissa Landeen said crews want restoration started quickly even though in many cases results won't show "for years down the line."
item.dc:creator: Alex Cabrero, KSL

item.title: Teen boys charged as adults for fatal Holladay shooting
item.description: Drake Preston Hernandez, 17, and Umda Woye Dike, 16, were charged as adults Friday with murder and obstruction of justice in the Oct. 15 shooting death of a man found in the parking area of Holladay's Chateau Foret condominiums, identified only as D.S. A tenant told police he heard an argument and then a single gunshot, and investigators found the victim, whose family said he had intellectual delay and severe social anxiety, holding a crumpled dollar bill with his backpack still zipped. Hernandez, who was arrested after his father called police, claimed the man followed them aggressively and that Dike's gun went off when Dike struck him with it.
item.dc:creator: Pat Reavy, KSL

item.title: Gavin Peterson's uncle speaks publicly as senator moves to revive child safety bill
item.description: Scott Peterson, uncle of 12-year-old Gavin Peterson, whose father Shane Peterson pleaded guilty to child abuse homicide in the boy's death, spoke publicly for the first time as Sen. Luz Escamilla plans to bring back the "Gavin Peterson Bill" in the 2027 session. The measure, SB 124, passed the Senate this year but died in the House; it would let juvenile court judges issue child safety warrants so DCFS workers and officers can physically see a child when credible abuse concerns exist but a family refuses access. Peterson said the family first assumed police had made a mistake and that the grief is worse knowing "someone you share blood with is the reason he is dead."
item.dc:creator: Garna Mejia, KSL

item.title: Safety company acknowledges hack seven months after breach exposed millions of crime tips
item.description: Navigate360 acknowledged Friday that hackers copied months of data from one of its systems, potentially exposing names, addresses, birth dates and Social Security numbers, seven months after a hacker claimed to have taken 93 gigabytes, including 8 million confidential tips, from its P3 Global Intel tip platform. The admission follows complaints from officials in Nevada and Canada that the company had shared only partial information, and Ontario police forces suspended the service after the CBC found hundreds of thousands of Canadian tipsters exposed.
item.dc:creator: Raphael Satter, Reuters

item.title: New accuser alleges abuse at the hands of former East Layton police officer
item.description: In an interview for KSL's COLD podcast, Gorgi Rigby, now 65, alleges that former East Layton reserve police officer Thomas "Tom" Jackson, a member of her ward, molested her in his patrol car in June 1975 after stopping her as a 14-year-old joyriding in her mother's car. The alleged encounter came within days of the July 4, 1975, disappearance of gas station attendant Nancy Perry Baird, a cold case in which the Davis County Sheriff's Office considers Jackson a "person of interest." Jackson, now incarcerated on later child sex abuse charges, did not respond, though letters he wrote from an Idaho prison years ago denied wrongdoing involving Rigby.
item.dc:creator: Dave Cawley, KSL

item.title: Erika Kirk moves for speedy trial as defense requests trial date 4 years after Charlie Kirk killed
item.description: Erika Kirk filed a victim's motion Thursday seeking a trial for Tyler Robinson as early as 2027, after his defense projected a seven-month capital trial starting in late 2029 and prosecutors proposed a 17-week trial beginning Jan. 31, 2028. Her counsel called the defense timeline "grossly out of line" with comparable Utah murder cases, accused it of using delay as a strategy, and warned it would cost taxpayers millions and feed conspiracy theories. The filing also asks Judge Tony Graf for monthly progress reports, noting the Kirks' children would be 7 and 5 by a verdict under the defense schedule.
item.dc:creator: Brigham Tomco, Deseret News

item.title: Is the surge in mortgage rates slowing?
item.description: Freddie Mac's weekly average for a 30-year fixed mortgage slipped to 7.32% from the 7.4% it had held for two weeks, but Fannie Mae's revised forecast now sees rates averaging 7.4% through year-end and 7.5% in 2027, up from the 6.8% it projected in September. Realtor.com estimated the past month's climb "wiped out $22,000 in home purchasing power" for a buyer budgeting $2,000 a month, while Redfin reported prices rising at their fastest annual pace since June 2025. Utah's median sales price reached $530,000 in September, 1.9% above a year earlier.
item.dc:creator: Lisa Riley Roche, Deseret News

item.title: For retirees, picking up a hobby could be the best thing for your mental health
item.description: The Bar None Wranglers, a St. George country band whose members are mostly in their 70s and 80s, have averaged about 140 shows a year over the past two years, many of them at memory care facilities, where band member Joe Lawrence says Alzheimer's patients who rarely speak start tapping their feet and singing along. Dennis Madsen joined after seeing the group four years ago, teaching himself ukulele, guitar and banjo from YouTube videos. Founder Robin Davis' advice to other retirees: "Whatever your passion is, do it — and it doesn't matter how many birthdays you have."
item.dc:creator: Tamara Vaifanua, KSL

item.title: Hurricane homeowners say this is the second round of severe floods in 2 months
item.description: Gould Wash overflowed Thursday and sent water into about 130 Hurricane homes, many of them flooded for the second time since August, and resident Marie Jessop said a changed creek bed made it "same flood, only worse this time." Volunteers bailed basements by bucket line, with one helper saying a basement that took about four feet of water two months ago had about seven this time. Mayor Clark Fawcett declared a local emergency so the city can seek state and federal cleanup funding.
item.dc:creator: Mike Anderson, KSL

item.title: 'Let my mom check my candy': Navigating Halloween with food allergies
item.description: Five of Syracuse mom Lasca Bennett's eight children have food allergies, so the family checks every Halloween treat at home before anyone eats, with 13-year-old Braellyn, once hospitalized after a red dye reaction, helping her siblings choose at the door. Primary Children's Hospital dietitian Linda Davila-Herrera advises reading labels even on familiar brands, since varieties of the same candy can differ, and teaching kids "Stop. Look. Ask. Go." She also suggests telling teachers and party hosts in advance, and households can offer nonfood treats through the Teal Pumpkin Project.
item.dc:creator: Emma Benson, KSL

item.title: Top education official warns against declaring the U. a 'sanctuary' campus for immigrant students
item.description: Utah System of Higher Education Commissioner Geoff Landward told University of Utah President Taylor Randall in a Sept. 30 letter that declaring the U. a sanctuary campus would be "inherently political" and therefore impermissible under the system's institutional neutrality guidance. Student government had backed Joint Resolution 10, which also seeks know-your-rights education and a pledge that campus police won't help enforce immigration law; trustees took no further action after board chair Katie Eccles summarized the letter. The student group MEChA de U of U says it remains committed to the cause and is working with administrators on the resolution's other demands.
item.dc:creator: Tim Vandenack, KSL

item.title: West Virginia investigates environmental groups over 'deceptive' climate change advocacy
item.description: West Virginia Attorney General JB McCuskey has subpoenaed a decade of fundraising and climate-advocacy records from the state's leading environmental groups, citing possible violations of the state's consumer protection law without detailing any alleged deception. The groups sued Thursday to quash the subpoenas, with an attorney for the West Virginia Rivers Coalition and 350.org calling them "a political action by the attorney general that is intended to stifle speech." The AP places the probe alongside similar Republican efforts, including a Florida subpoena of the Environmental Law Institute, and Georgetown law professor David Cole called it "frivolous."
item.dc:creator: Jim Mustian and Sarah Rankin, Associated Press

item.title: Pediatrician warns about energy drink risks for teens
item.description: Idaho Falls pediatrician Dr. Todd L. Jacobs says he regularly sees teens drinking energy drinks, some as many as three a day, and notes that a single can of Reign or Bang holds 300 milligrams of caffeine, about two Monsters' worth. His main worry is a cycle of poor sleep followed by more caffeine the next day, along with anxiety, palpitations, mood swings and medications that can magnify caffeine's effects. Citing American Academy of Pediatrics guidance that energy drinks aren't appropriate for kids, he urged parents to watch caffeine intake, including from pre-workout powders, noting "The teen years are just hard."
item.dc:creator: Todd Kunz, KSL

item.title: SK Hynix says Solidigm drops plan for US IPO amid market volatility
item.description: SK Hynix has dropped plans for a U.S. initial public offering of Solidigm, its Rancho Cordova, California-based NAND flash and solid-state drive subsidiary, citing market volatility and a broader pullback in chip stocks. The company said the decision "does not reflect any change in Solidigm's growth prospects or investment needs" and that it will look at other ways to fund expansion amid AI-driven memory demand. SK Hynix had argued a listing would raise outside capital for new plants and help investors value Solidigm more fully.
item.dc:creator: Reuters

item.title: Charges dismissed against ex-Ogden officer in July 4 incident that allegedly injured 8 people
item.description: All nine charges against former Ogden police officer Tyler Allen Crouch, 49, were dismissed Monday, court records show, with no explanation given; prosecutors did not immediately respond and his attorney declined comment. Crouch had been accused of speeding out of a lot near Ogden-Hinckley Airport amid a July 4 fireworks crowd and hitting a parked car that was pushed into another, injuring eight people, including an 11-year-old girl who was "sandwiched" between vehicles. The charges, mostly third-degree felonies, included DUI with two prior convictions in 10 years and negligently causing serious bodily injury.
item.dc:creator: Tim Vandenack, KSL

item.title: Trump blasts 76ers star LeBron James as 'disgrace' for not standing still during national anthem
item.description: President Donald Trump called LeBron James "a TOTAL DISGRACE" and demanded an apology after video showed the 41-year-old, now with the Philadelphia 76ers, apparently practicing a golf swing and jump shot during the national anthem before the team's season opener at Madison Square Garden. James had not responded by Thursday afternoon, and coach Nick Nurse called it more "outside noise" before James' home debut. The two have traded barbs for years, with James repeatedly vowing to keep speaking out on social and political issues.
item.dc:creator: Dan Gelston, Associated Press

item.title: Five ways to keep safe online in the wake of AI-supercharged hacking
item.description: After the disclosure of hackable flaws in PHP, the language behind roughly 70% of websites, security experts told Reuters that AI models are making long-hidden software bugs easier to find and exploit, and that most of the burden falls on companies to patch faster. For individuals, they recommend multi-factor authentication, unique passwords or passkeys, automatic updates for phones, computers, routers and smart-home devices, and skepticism toward urgent "secure your account" messages. Trail of Bits CEO Dan Guido noted the limits of personal precautions: "You can't patch your hospital's website."
item.dc:creator: AJ Vicens, Reuters

item.title: Hurricane declares emergency over flooding; warning for many areas near Lake Powell
item.description: Hurricane Mayor Clark Fawcett declared a local emergency Thursday after flooding along Gould Wash affected about 80 homes and 50 RVs at Willow Wind RV Park, damaged bridges, culverts and roads, and forced evacuations; the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints opened a stake center as a shelter. The National Weather Service had warned of a "large flood wave" after 1 to 2 inches of rain fell on the wash's headwaters, and it issued a rare, expansive flood warning across southeast and south-central Utah, including all of Glen Canyon National Recreation Area and Lake Powell. Flood debris also closed part of state Route 24 in Capitol Reef National Park, with storms expected statewide before drier weather this weekend.
item.dc:creator: Carter Williams, KSL

item.title: Gilead to buy PepStar's inflammation drug program in $1.28 billion deal
item.description: Gilead Sciences will pay $1.275 billion in cash upfront for PepStar Therapeutics' oral inflammation program, including HCXT-2001, an experimental inflammatory bowel disease pill designed to block the IL-23 receptor, days after positive mid-stage results for its own bowel-disease drug emvistegrast. Citi analyst Geoffrey Meacham called the price notable because HCXT-2001 is in early testing with no published clinical data, though he said it extends Gilead's push beyond its core HIV business. The deal, which gives Gilead worldwide rights, is expected to close this quarter.
item.dc:creator: Sahil Pandey, Reuters

item.title: Merck/Moderna cancer vaccine cuts melanoma death or recurrence risk by 42%, shares fall
item.description: In a Phase 3 trial of more than 1,100 patients, Moderna and Merck's personalized mRNA vaccine intismeran autogene, given with Merck's immunotherapy Keytruda after melanoma surgery, cut the risk of death or recurrence by 42% and of spread by 38%; 82.2% of patients were cancer-free after two years, versus 70% on Keytruda alone. Moderna CEO Stephane Bancel said the companies will seek U.S. approval and expect a 2027 launch, and the combination is already being tested in kidney, bladder and lung cancer. Moderna shares, which had nearly quadrupled since August, closed more than 17% lower after the data leaked, as some analysts questioned how broadly the approach will extend; RBC's Trung Huynh wrote that "melanoma was supposed to be the best case."
item.dc:creator: Michael Erman and Julie Steenhuysen, Reuters

item.title: Hanksville businesses feeling effects of lower water levels at Lake Powell
item.description: Business owners in Hanksville, a Wayne County town that depends on travelers headed to Lake Powell's Bullfrog Marina, say summer business fell to "probably half what we should have been," according to Jessica Alvey, whose family runs several local businesses including Stan's Burger Shak. Alvey partly blames coverage of the reservoir's low levels, noting that visitors who came anyway found beaches, trails and hikes that had long been underwater. Town councilmember Shyann Alvey said the town is budgeting cautiously and has formed a business coalition to promote nearby draws such as Goblin Valley State Park and Capitol Reef National Park.
item.dc:creator: Alex Cabrero, KSL

item.title: DOJ to send election monitors to Utah, lieutenant governor says
item.description: The U.S. Justice Department told Lt. Gov. Deidre Henderson it will send election monitors to "one or more jurisdictions" in Utah on Nov. 3 without saying where or how many, and Henderson said they must follow state poll-watcher rules, will not approach voters or carry weapons, and will identify themselves to poll workers. "I welcome people looking and examining, what I don't welcome is any kind of interference," Henderson said, adding she plans to meet with the regional director beforehand. Utah Democratic Party Chair Brian King condemned the move as federal intimidation of voters; the department has previously sent poll watchers to San Juan County in four elections since 2016.
item.dc:creator: Joe R. Wirthlin Jr, KSL

item.title: Millions in cheese revenue lost as protest torpedoes Italy's buffalo mozzarella output
item.description: A weeklong truckers' strike in southern Italy over diesel prices driven up by the Iran war stopped buffalo mozzarella production, leaving about 1 million liters of milk unprocessed and causing what consortium director Pier Maria Saccani called a "3 million-euro block in 24 hours." Because buffalo milk must become mozzarella within 60 hours and farms can't store much of it, several dairies have closed and some farmers are feeding unused milk to their animals. Premier Giorgia Meloni's government approved expanded fuel tax credits for truckers and farmers Thursday, though it was unclear whether that would end the protest.
item.dc:creator: Giada Zampano, Associated Press

item.title: This 'hidden gem' in Arizona just became America's newest national park
item.description: President Donald Trump signed a law Tuesday redesignating Arizona's Chiricahua National Monument, nicknamed the "Wonderland of Rocks," as the nation's 64th national park and Arizona's fourth, protecting about 12,000 acres of volcanic landscape formed some 27 million years ago. Arizona Sen. Mark Kelly, who first introduced the Chiricahua National Park Act in 2021, called the signing "a historic day for Arizona." Interior Secretary Doug Burgum said the new status should draw more visitors to the area, roughly 120 miles from Tucson, and help local economies.
item.dc:creator: Emily Walker, Deseret News

item.title: The connection between having in-person friends and problematic social media use
item.description: A study of 555 U.S. adults published in PLOS One found that people with a "fearful" attachment style, anxious about relationships and inclined to avoid them, are most likely to use social media in ways that interfere with work or school, while securely attached people have the lowest problematic use. Lead author Chris Bjornsen of Longwood University said the findings show association, not causation, and suggested people check whether social media is hurting their performance and consider quitting or sharply cutting back. Therapist Kimberly Solo, who was not involved in the study, said relationship skills are learned and can be built as an adult: "Awareness is the first step."
item.dc:creator: Kara Alaimo, CNN

item.title: Third gunman sentenced in deadly shooting at Weber County street racing competition
item.description: Christian Elias Antonio Ruiz, 17 at the time of an Aug. 31, 2025, shooting at an illegal street race in rural western Weber County that killed 22-year-old Jesus Cuadras Garcia, was sentenced to one to 15 years in prison for manslaughter, plus consecutive time on two firearms counts, under a plea deal that reduced a murder charge. Ruiz, the last of three gunmen to be sentenced, wrote to the judge that he is "ashamed of what I did." Co-defendant Michael Robles Gaisbauer received prison terms in May, and a third shooter, 15 at the time, was ordered held in juvenile detention until age 25.
item.dc:creator: Tim Vandenack, KSL

item.title: Daughters of serial child sex offender speak out on behalf of victims
item.description: KSL's COLD podcast details the November 2025 sentencing of Thomas Richard Jackson, 79, a former East Layton police officer whose daughters Heidi Holmberg and Tori Riddle reported 1980s abuse to Davis County detectives after hearing him on a 2023 COLD episode. Judge Michael DiReda imposed consecutive prison terms, the maximum allowed, and called the sentencing guidelines' option of jail plus probation "an absolute mockery of justice" that shows the Legislature underrates crimes against children. Jackson, a repeat offender previously convicted in Utah and Idaho and a person of interest in the 1975 disappearance of Nancy Perry Baird, has not been charged in that case, and COLD reports more potential victims have since come forward.
item.dc:creator: Dave Cawley, KSL

item.title: Violent Arizona storms bring possible tornado, toppled trees and golf ball-size hail
item.description: Severe storms swept northern and central Arizona overnight into Thursday, with a possible tornado in Heber-Overgaard, a Navajo County community of about 3,000, uprooting trees, damaging structures and causing minor injuries, while golf ball-size hail broke windows and dented cars elsewhere. State Rep. Walt Blackman requested an emergency declaration, and members of Overgaard Baptist Church sheltered in a restroom as the storm hit their prayer meeting. A Flagstaff meteorologist said the storms, fed by warm, moist air, were "very unusual for this area at this time of the year," toppling ponderosa pines over 30 feet tall in the Coconino National Forest.
item.dc:creator: Wufei Yu and Jessica Hill, Associated Press

item.title: First Presbyterian Church to host 40th annual Scottish heritage events
item.description: Salt Lake City's First Presbyterian Church holds its 40th annual Scottish Festival on Saturday, with free family activities and an evening concert by the Salt Lake Scots Pipe Band, followed Sunday by the Kirkin' o' th' Tartan, a Reformation Sunday tradition in which pastors bless Scottish-American families' clan tartans. Pastor Jamie White said the Sunday services drew as many as 1,700 people last year, and when the band plays "Amazing Grace" afterward, "There's not a dry eye in the room." Baked-goods proceeds will go to the Pamela Atkinson Resource Center and other charities, honoring the longtime church member and advocate who died Oct. 10 at 93.
item.dc:creator: Joe R. Wirthlin Jr, KSL

item.title: Judge orders Trump to sit for a deposition in his defamation lawsuit against the BBC by Dec. 11
item.description: A federal magistrate judge in Miami ordered President Donald Trump to sit for a deposition by Dec. 11 in his $10 billion defamation suit against the BBC or face sanctions up to dismissal, after the broadcaster's lawyer said Trump canceled an agreed Oct. 16 date and campaigned in Georgia instead. The suit centers on a documentary that the BBC admits spliced together parts of Trump's Jan. 6, 2021, speech; the network apologized but denies defamation. The two sides are also fighting over the BBC's subpoena of former special counsel Jack Smith, whom its lawyers called the most "authoritative source" on Jan. 6 and whom Trump's team says lacks relevant personal knowledge.
item.dc:creator: David Fischer, Associated Press

item.title: Ogden man accused of threatening synagogue in 2025 charged with federal hate crime
item.description: Federal prosecutors have indicted Skyler AJ Rose, 22, of Ogden on hate crime, explosives and child sexual abuse material charges, alleging he posted threats in December 2025 to kill Jews and "blow up a synagogue," searched for directions to an Ogden synagogue, and kept six functional homemade pipe bombs at home. U.S. Attorney Melissa Holyoak said a place of worship "should be a refuge of safety, not fear," and prosecutors are seeking his detention, noting the alleged threats came while he was on a plea in abeyance for firing a homemade shotgun in public. Rose also faces 14 felonies in a pending state case.
item.dc:creator: Cassidy Wixom, KSL

item.title: Utah man pleads guilty to killing ex-girlfriend, will not contest sentence of life without parole
item.description: Jacob Holt Johnson, 42, of Herriman, pleaded guilty to aggravated murder Thursday in the December 2024 strangling of his ex-girlfriend Summer Tatiana Roney, telling the court, "I caused the death of Summer." Under the deal he agreed to a sentence of life without parole, prosecutors dropped the death penalty and other charges after consulting her family, and a judge will impose sentence on Dec. 17. Roney's relatives, who had said they would accept a plea only with life without parole, wept in court and plan to speak at sentencing.
item.dc:creator: Emily Ashcraft, KSL

item.title: Shark nicknamed 'Bukangi' foils rescue attempts, returns to South Korean canal
item.description: A 10-foot female dusky shark nicknamed "Bukangi" slipped back into a Busan canal a day after South Korean authorities spent hours guiding her to the open sea, swimming beneath a net and ending up between two barriers. Since she was spotted late last month the endangered shark has drawn about 1.6 million visitors, and officials opened the outer net hoping she will leave on her own while they monitor her stable condition. Experts link more frequent shark sightings along South Korea's east coast to warming ocean temperatures.
item.dc:creator: Maggie Grether and Hyun Young Yi, Reuters

item.title: Elizabeth Smart kidnapper waives preliminary hearing for park charges, is working on settlement
item.description: Wanda Eileen Barzee, 80, who served her full sentence for her role in the 2002 kidnapping of Elizabeth Smart, waived a preliminary hearing Thursday on two misdemeanor counts of being a sex offender in a protected area, filed after she visited Liberty Park and Sugar House Park. Barzee has acknowledged going to the parks to sit on benches and feed ducks, saying she was "commanded to by the Lord." Her attorney, Scott Williams, said a settlement is likely; her next hearing is set for Jan. 15, 2027.
item.dc:creator: Emily Ashcraft, KSL

item.title: Utah legislative hearing focuses on accuracy of water funding study following KSL Investigation
item.description: At a legislative hearing that followed a KSL Investigators report, lawmakers and utility officials challenged a roughly $170,000 state-commissioned study whose $1.2 billion annual water infrastructure estimate underpinned HB501, a 2026 bill that would have pressed suppliers to collect more revenue, because it never asked about utilities' existing revenues or reserves. Rep. James Dunnigan said the results appear "flawed," and West Jordan's Danyce Steck compared the state's request to a child's Sears catalog wish list. A Division of Water Resources official said the agency has largely moved past the $1.2 billion figure toward a two-year state need of about $300 million, while the Utah Rivers Council said 76 suppliers it reviewed reported nearly $780 million in net revenue.
item.dc:creator: Daniella Rivera, KSL

item.title: Besi beats order forecasts, says ASML not a hybrid bonding rival
item.description: Dutch chip-equipment maker BE Semiconductor Industries reported third-quarter orders of €342.6 million, nearly double a year earlier and well above analyst forecasts, on AI data-center demand, and announced a new €100 million share buyback. CEO Richard Blickman rejected a SemiAnalysis report that had hit Besi's shares, saying "We do not view ASML as a hybrid bonding competitor" and that the two companies are working together. Besi guided fourth-quarter revenue roughly flat, below expectations, which Blickman attributed to the timing of customers' production lines rather than delays.
item.dc:creator: Nathan Vifflin, Reuters

item.title: Grantsville neighbors pleading for help after years of flooding
item.description: Residents of Grantsville's Wells Crossing subdivision used public comment at a City Council meeting to press for drainage fixes after a Sept. 18 storm flooded about 10 homes, saying runoff from an adjacent field and an unfinished section of Nygreen Street has caused repeated flooding for years. Homeowners who combed city and county records say a planned drainage swale and check dams were never built, and newcomer Kerry Jones estimated "more than 50 houses over the past five years" have had problems. Resident Wes Russell said the city should fix the neighborhood before approving thousands of additional homes, and speakers asked for the issue to be placed on a formal meeting agenda.
item.dc:creator: Shelby Lofton, KSL

item.title: Micron unveils global profit-linked bonus plan after Taiwan union pressure
item.description: Idaho-based Micron Technology will add quarterly profit-linked payments for employees worldwide starting in fiscal 2027, after Taiwan unions pushed for a bigger share of AI-driven earnings; the pool is based on after-tax profit minus next-quarter capital spending, paid half in cash and half in shares. Unlike Samsung and SK Hynix, which set aside fixed shares of profit, Micron disclosed no percentage, and a union in Taoyuan that wants 15% of operating profit has yet to accept the offer, though one in Taichung reached a deal. For its roughly 15,000 Taiwan workers, Micron is also raising retirement contributions to 10%, adding three paid days off and tripling the day-shift allowance.
item.dc:creator: Wen-Yee Lee, Reuters

item.title: Leaders of church fear historic Japantown will remain 'Japandock' despite Smith's vision
item.description: Members of the Japanese Church of Christ and Salt Lake Buddhist Temple, the last remnants of Salt Lake City's historic Japantown along 100 South, fear that construction for Smith Entertainment Group's planned downtown district could damage the 102-year-old church's foundation and leave the street as the district's "back of house." Church elder Lynne Ward said trucks serving the planned 6,000-seat Live Nation venue would block the street's Japanese-themed art and bring back what locals called "Japandock." SEG executive Mike Maughan said plans are still changing, that the company already removed 400 feet of exposed loading docks at the churches' request, and that it will monitor the church's foundation during digging.
item.dc:creator: Carter Williams, KSL

item.title: Tyler Robinson doesn't anticipate trial until 2029
item.description: In filings ahead of a Friday scheduling conference, Tyler Robinson's defense team said a capital trial in the killing of Charlie Kirk at Utah Valley University might start in the third quarter of 2029 and last six to seven months, citing evidence still being processed, motions planned through early 2027, the difficulty of seating a jury and a possible change-of-venue request. Utah County prosecutors instead proposed starting a 17-week trial on Jan. 31, 2028. Separately, 4th District Judge Tony Graf denied the defense's bid to bar a Deseret News photographer from the hearing, which Erika Kirk will be allowed to attend remotely.
item.dc:creator: Pat Reavy, KSL

item.title: Orem to host Ironman 70.3, drawing athletes and visitors to Utah County
item.description: Orem will host the inaugural IRONMAN 70.3 Utah next August, the city's first IRONMAN-branded race, with a 1.2-mile swim in Deer Creek Reservoir, a 56-mile ride through Provo Canyon and a 13.1-mile run through Orem. City spokesman Pete Wolfley said officials expect thousands of visitors over the next three years and "estimated millions of dollars of economic benefit to the city." Local triathlete Heather Jenson, a veteran of eight half-IRONMAN races, said she expects the event to sell out and urged non-racers to volunteer.
item.dc:creator: Annette Campbell, KSL

item.title: Family of slain Utah woman supports plea deal if it includes life without parole
item.description: Ahead of a preliminary hearing for Jacob Holt Johnson, 42, charged with aggravated murder in the death of 30-year-old Summer Tatiana Roney, whose body was found in a box in a Jeep at a Bluffdale 7-Eleven on Dec. 31, 2024, her sister Michelle Tischner said the family would accept a plea deal only with "Nothing less than life without parole." Tischner, who was Roney's legal guardian, said her sister had cognitive limitations, describing her as "forever 12," and believes Johnson preyed on her. Salt Lake County District Attorney Sim Gill would not discuss negotiations but said prosecutors stay open to any outcome.
item.dc:creator: Garna Mejia, KSL

item.title: Utah lawmakers eye permanently allowing motorcycle lane filtering
item.description: Utah's Transportation Interim Committee advanced a bill from Rep. Walt Brooks, R-St. George, that would make motorcycle lane filtering permanent before the current law expires next year and allow it in stopped traffic on roads posted up to 55 mph, while still barring it on I-15 and I-215. The bill would also permit side-mounted amber lights and let courts require rider education for violators, though Reps. Norm Thurston and Ariel Defay said they would rather revisit the law every few years. The debate follows a record 72 motorcycle deaths in Utah last year; a Highway Patrol official said earlier this year the law "hasn't had very much of an effect in making things more safe or more dangerous."
item.dc:creator: Daniel Woodruff, KSL

item.title: Utah lawmakers paid for a study on mail-in voting security. Here's what researchers found
item.description: A Legislature-commissioned study by Utah Valley University's Gary R. Herbert Institute for Public Policy found "no evidence of significant or widespread fraud" in Utah elections; all 51 alleged Utah cases in national fraud databases for 2000-2019 traced to a single 2006 Daggett County mayoral race, and the shift to vote-by-mail raised turnout, especially in rural counties. Asked how voters returning mail ballots could be made to show ID, researchers said the only option meeting lawmakers' full requirements would be paid poll workers at every drop box, costing about $8 million a year and stretching drop-off time from one to four minutes per voter. The report urged lawmakers to weigh changes against existing safeguards and not to move too quickly.
item.dc:creator: Bridger Beal-Cvetko, KSL

item.title: USU Extension fact sheet helps adults recognize and respond to youth trauma
item.description: Utah State University Extension has turned years of research into a fact sheet, "Understanding and Supporting Youth Affected by Trauma and Stress," written for teachers, coaches and other adults who work with young people. Co-author Cara Murray, a professional practice assistant professor, said warning signs such as withdrawal, skipped practices or emotional outbursts are easy to mistake for misbehavior, and that the same hardship, from bullying to family instability, can affect two young people very differently. She said adults don't need clinical training to help, since a stable setting and patience build trust: "We are not there to diagnose. We are there to listen."
item.dc:creator: Todd Kunz, KSL

item.title: USU researchers tap machine learning, game cameras to inform recreation area management
item.description: Utah State University's Institute of Outdoor Recreation and Tourism Management tested a way to measure crowding with the U.S. Forest Service on Idaho's Payette River corridor, mapping parking supply from aerial imagery and using computer vision on nearly a half-million game-camera photos to count vehicles and watercraft. Director Jordan Smith said parking is "the critical pitch point" for outdoor trips, and the data shows managers where and when sites hit capacity, analysis he said once filled a graduate student's master's thesis but now takes hours. The institute is starting a similar project with Cache County and has launched a Recreation Capacity Platform with dashboards combining maps, camera counts and conditions.
item.dc:creator: Logan Stefanich, KSL

item.title: Utah higher education institutions provide value, students leave money on table, economist says
item.description: At a Kem C. Gardner Policy Institute panel, University of Tennessee economist Michael Kofoed said Utah's colleges offer "incredible value and an incredibly low price to the student," since few students pay the sticker price and average per-student grant aid ranges from $5,972 at Snow College to $12,744 at the University of Utah. The catch is that only 42.3% of Utah's 2025 high school seniors completed the FAFSA, second-lowest in the nation after Alaska, so students forgo millions in Pell Grants and aid such as the Utah Promise Scholarship. Asked to describe the sector's future in one word, Utah Commissioner of Higher Education Geoffrey Landward chose "transformation."
item.dc:creator: Logan Stefanich, KSL

item.title: Russia frees retired US schoolteacher in goodwill gesture as Putin meets Witkoff
item.description: Russia released Stephen Hubbard, a 74-year-old retired U.S. schoolteacher held since 2022, after President Vladimir Putin met U.S. envoy Steve Witkoff in Saint Petersburg in talks Washington described as a step toward ending the war in Ukraine. Witkoff's description of Putin as a "humanitarian" drew bipartisan criticism, including from Republican Sen. Thom Tillis. President Donald Trump said the U.S. gave nothing in return, and Norway's prime minister said another three-way meeting of Washington, Moscow and Kyiv will likely take place in mid-November.
item.dc:creator: Lucy Papachristou, Reuters

item.title: Residents cited after physical altercation over data center discussion in Utah County meeting
item.description: A Utah County Planning Commission meeting on a just-passed ordinance creating a process to approve or deny data centers on unincorporated land ended with deputies removing a protester, Aspen Azalea, 27, who said she suffered a concussion. The sheriff's office said she struck a deputy in the groin and two others grabbed her; she was booked for investigation of assaulting a peace officer, and the other two were cited. Sheriff Mike Smith said his office respects free speech while maintaining public order.
item.dc:creator: KSL Staff

item.title: UTA updates its 30-year transit plan and looks for input from Utahns
item.description: Utah Transit Authority is taking public comments through Nov. 30 on its "UTA moves 2055" long-range plan, which it revises every four years, with an eye toward events such as the 2034 Winter Olympics. Spokesman Gavin Gustafson said every comment is analyzed to set priorities, with any expansion depending on demand and funding.
item.dc:creator: Allison Lyons and Paige Zamora, KSL

item.title: 'I just, lost control,' Utah man convicted of child abuse homicide tells parole board
item.description: Gregory Todd Fullerton, 49, convicted of child abuse homicide in the 2008 death of his fiancée's 4-month-old son, Nicholas "Nicky" Long, told the Utah Board of Pardons and Parole at his first hearing that he killed the infant "in a fit of rage." The boy's mother, Samantha, said she remains heartbroken and argued it would be unfair for Fullerton to be released. The board noted his good prison disciplinary record, and the full five-member board will decide on parole.
item.dc:creator: Pat Reavy, KSL

item.title: Wasatch County sheriff placed on paid leave, seeks new judge in Richins investigation case
item.description: Wasatch County Sheriff Jared Rigby, charged earlier this month with felony obstruction over alleged interference in the Richins investigation, took voluntary paid administrative leave and asked to disqualify the judge in his case, saying the judge has "personal knowledge of facts that are in dispute." The County Council unanimously dropped a resolution calling for his resignation and accepted the leave, with the undersheriff running the office through year's end. Rigby, who is not seeking reelection, had refused a county offer to pay out the rest of his term if he resigned.
item.dc:creator: Cassidy Wixom, KSL

item.title: Tooele County balloon handler to fulfill livelong dream in 100th Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade
item.description: Alex Harris, 18, of Lake Point in Tooele County, will be a balloon handler in the 100th Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade, a goal he has held since first watching the parade at age 4. He has trained by walking miles and lifting weights and practiced twice in New Jersey, including a windy session that showed how much effort the job takes. "This has been a dream of mine for so many years," said Harris, who will learn his balloon assignment in early November.
item.dc:creator: Joe R. Wirthlin Jr, KSL

item.title: Germany's SAP hits €10 billion quarterly revenue milestone, lifts 2026 view
item.description: SAP posted its first €10 billion revenue quarter, with cloud revenue and current cloud backlog both up 26%, and said 2026 revenue should land at the top of its forecast range. CEO Christian Klein said "AI was the main driver" of customers' moves to the cloud, as companies subscribe for access to its Joule assistant platform. CFO Dominik Asam cautioned that the fourth quarter will decide the year amid rising oil prices and U.S. interest rates.
item.dc:creator: Leo Marchandon, Reuters

item.title: Trump awards Utahn Nick Shirley $10K check under new anti-fraud reward program
item.description: President Donald Trump gave Farmington native Nick Shirley, 24, a $10,000 check for his viral videos alleging Minnesota child care fraud as the White House launched a Fraud Whistleblower Incentive Program. The Justice Department-run program, starting with $25 million, can pay whistleblowers 1% of funds recovered once fraud is proved through a conviction or other federal enforcement action. Shirley also called a California law dubbed the "Stop Nick Shirley Act" a "direct violation of the First Amendment."
item.dc:creator: Lauren Irwin, Deseret News

item.title: Tesla posts surprise positive cash flow on lower-than-expected AI spending
item.description: Tesla reported $1.53 billion in third-quarter free cash flow, versus an expected cash burn, after capital spending of $4.7 billion came in well under the $7.5 billion analysts forecast, while revenue of $28.05 billion also beat estimates. The results come as Elon Musk calls a Tesla-SpaceX merger a "good idea," though one analyst said the lower capex "suggests less of an 'all-in' approach to the AI arms race." Tesla delivered 486,532 vehicles and said it ended the quarter with its largest passenger-vehicle backlog in four years.
item.dc:creator: Akash Sriram and Abhirup Roy, Reuters

item.title: Southwest Airlines cuts profit forecast as fuel costs overshadow turnaround gains
item.description: Southwest Airlines cut its 2026 adjusted earnings forecast to $2.60 to $2.85 per share from $3.25 to $4.25 as a fuel bill up $821 million from a year earlier offset gains from its business overhaul. Average fares rose nearly 27% in the third quarter, lifting revenue to a record $8.4 billion, and adjusted earnings of 66 cents a share beat estimates. "With the transformation complete," CEO Bob Jordan said, the airline is now focused on optimizing the business.
item.dc:creator: Rajesh Kumar Singh and Nandan Mandayam, Reuters

item.title: Pope Leo will not need further therapy after his operation, doctors say
item.description: Doctors for Pope Leo said Wednesday that the 71-year-old pontiff needs no further treatment after the Oct. 13 removal of the lower lobe of his right lung, with tissue analysis confirming a lung adenocarcinoma that remained localized. "A subsequent oncological evaluation has confirmed that no further therapy is required," his lead surgeon and personal physician said. Leo has resumed his weekly audience in St Peter's Square, though it is still unclear whether he will make a planned Nov. 6-17 trip to Uruguay, Argentina and Peru.
item.dc:creator: Reuters

item.title: Walmart launches tools for AI agents to shop for customers
item.description: Walmart is opening its business to AI shopping agents, with "Agent Profiles" arriving next month that let customers authorize specific agents, cap their spending or require sign-off, and cut off access at any time. Its new "Walmart Agent Gateway" plugs assistants including ChatGPT, Gemini and Meta's Muse into Walmart and Sam's Club search and checkout, while keeping payment card data out of agents' reach. The move sets Walmart apart from Amazon, which has tried to restrict outside shopping agents, and requires no Walmart+ membership.
item.dc:creator: Sanskriti Shekhar, Reuters

item.title: Some websites go dark as operators address an AI-detected flaw in a web programming language
item.description: The FBI's cyber division warned that newly disclosed PHP vulnerabilities could let attackers remotely execute code and advised taking sites offline if they cannot be updated right away; Finland's government websites were among those left partly unavailable. OpenAI said it led a coalition including Wiz and Cloudflare that worked on the flaws for two months, calling them "one of the most impactful security issues in recent memory" and expecting similar AI-found bugs to "increase sharply in the coming months." Arctic Wolf's Ismael Valenzuela said PHP runs roughly 70% of websites whose server-side language is known.
item.dc:creator: Barbara Ortutay, Associated Press

item.title: Utah Apple Crunch connects kindergarteners with local farmers
item.description: Utah's annual Apple Crunch brought about 150 Canyons School District kindergarteners to the state Capitol to learn how apples get from local orchards to their lunch trays. The event, started in 2017 for National Farm to School Month, is meant to build healthy eating habits, said Silver Mesa Elementary teacher Chelsea Prime, and ties into a month of farm-focused school activities statewide.
item.dc:creator: Madi Vollmer, KSL

item.title: New Utah Supreme Court justice signed Proposition 4 repeal petition
item.description: Utah Supreme Court Justice Michael Menssen, appointed in August, signed a Feb. 12 petition seeking to overturn the anti-gerrymandering Proposition 4 but has not recused himself from redistricting litigation now before the court. Gov. Spencer Cox's office said "We were not aware," noting petition signatures are not part of its merit review, and Menssen apparently did not disclose his support when interviewed. Alliance for a Better Utah has called for his recusal, while a courts spokesperson said normal recusal standards were followed.
item.dc:creator: Bridger Beal-Cvetko and Daniel Woodruff, KSL

item.title: Christina Applegate, a leading MS advocate, says doctors found she doesn't have the disease after all
item.description: Christina Applegate, a prominent multiple sclerosis advocate since her 2021 diagnosis, said on her podcast that new testing has ruled out MS, leaving her "back at square one" on explaining her ongoing symptoms. Cedars-Sinai neurologist Dr. Marwa Kaisey, a guest on the episode, co-authored research showing nearly 1 in 5 patients referred with an MS label fell short of the disease's diagnostic criteria. Applegate's illness had forced her to leave the Netflix series "Dead to Me."
item.dc:creator: Lisa Respers France, CNN

item.title: State Bank of India reports cyberattack involving nearly 3,900 customer records
item.description: Personal data tied to 3,897 State Bank of India customers, including loan records, contact details and birth dates, surfaced on the dark web, the lender disclosed, adding that "Customer balances are completely safe." SBI has brought in an independent security firm and sees no material hit to its business, as India's banking regulator presses lenders to harden cyber defenses.
item.dc:creator: Reuters

item.title: Government websites go dark after AI-discovered flaw sparks security scramble
item.description: Government agencies across Europe, the Dutch cybersecurity agency and some Wikipedia systems went offline as a precaution after PHP developers released urgent fixes for long-hidden critical flaws that were uncovered with AI. Experts warned AI tools can quickly reverse engineer the patch, with TLP:Black co-founder Costin Raiu predicting the "mass compromise of every vulnerable web server on the internet." Censys data showed about 1.5 million of 2.6 million hosts running a PHP version with no fix, and Drupal Association interim CEO Tiffany Farriss said "This issue impacts the majority of the Internet."
item.dc:creator: Raphael Satter, Leo Marchandon, Kanjyik Ghosh and Rajveer Pardesi, Reuters

item.title: 'Sacrificed his life for everyone ... to be shot point blank,' victim's family says at parole hearing
item.description: Colton James Beed, 27, who pleaded guilty to manslaughter in the 2019 killing of Marine veteran Mason Hunt during a burglary targeting a marijuana dealer's Salt Lake City home, called it a "dumb decision" at his first parole hearing. Hunt was shot after returning home and putting one intruder in a headlock, having been called by a housemate hiding in a bathtub. His sister LauraKay Hunt, who has spoken at hearings for codefendants, two of whom were paroled, rejected Beed's explanation that he was high.
item.dc:creator: Pat Reavy, KSL

item.title: Anthropic unveils Claude Duet AI agent app
item.description: Anthropic's new Claude Duet app is meant to act before it is asked, scanning a user's connected apps to flag what needs attention and taking on work such as meeting scheduling, financial forecasting and building web apps. The research preview, built on Opus 5.5, is limited to waitlisted U.S. Pro and Max subscribers and can tap more than 6,000 Claude Marketplace connectors and pay via Stripe's Link or Shopify's Shop Pay. Anthropic requires approval for sensitive actions and concedes Duet is weaker on personal errands like ticket booking, as OpenAI and Meta race out their own agents.
item.dc:creator: Reuters

item.title: Former proposed ICE detention center site in Salt Lake now up for sale
item.description: The 6020 W. 300 South warehouse that ICE bought for $145.44 million in March to convert into an immigrant detention center is now listed for sale by Cushman and Wakefield with six other former proposed sites as a "Federal Warehouse Portfolio." A federal magistrate in Salt Lake City and County's lawsuit extended the deadline for a sale status report to Jan. 18 and barred any conversion during the stay. Federal officials say they still intend to dispose of the property, which remains in federal hands.
item.dc:creator: Tim Vandenack, KSL

item.title: 'I couldn't imagine doing that to my child,' woman says of father sent to prison
item.description: Robert Quentin Sprague, 65, accused of falsely claiming his wife was plotting to kill him and of breaking into her southern Utah home days after his release, received suspended prison terms, probation and a year in jail after pleading guilty to identity fraud, forgery and witness tampering. Fifth District Judge Eric Gentry called him a liar and manipulative and imposed more jail time than either side recommended. His adult daughter, who called the outcome "a slap on the wrist," hopes to draw attention to non-spousal domestic violence.
item.dc:creator: Pat Reavy, KSL

item.title: US is a big reason for the world losing ground in the fight against climate change, UN report says
item.description: A United Nations Environment Programme update projects Earth will warm another 2.2 degrees Fahrenheit even if nations meet their pledges, about two-tenths of a degree more than last year's estimate, citing the U.S. withdrawal from the Paris Agreement and revised historical emissions. The report found U.S. emissions rose 133 megatons in 2025, about 70% of the increase among countries whose emissions grew, driven by electricity demand and a coal rebound. Climate Analytics CEO Bill Hare said the U.S. is "looking at the fire, denying there is a fire, and then pouring more petrol on it."
item.dc:creator: Seth Borenstein, Associated Press

item.title: Davis County opens ballot-counting process to public view
item.description: Davis County Clerk Brian McKenzie has moved ballot-processing operations to within six feet of large windows at his Farmington office so the public can watch mail ballots being handled as early voting gets underway. "People can get up close and watch what's happening," McKenzie said, adding that in 20 years at the county only five noncitizens had been found registered, all since removed. The county has more than 200,000 active voters and expects about 60% turnout, mostly by mail ballot.
item.dc:creator: Garna Mejia, KSL

item.title: Supreme Court won't allow Trump administration restrictions on transgender inmates
item.description: The Supreme Court denied the Trump administration's emergency request to enforce a Federal Bureau of Prisons policy barring gender-affirming medical treatment and "social accommodations" for transgender inmates while a class action proceeds, with Justices Clarence Thomas and Samuel Alito dissenting. The February policy would reverse hormone treatment the federal prison system has provided since at least 1992, according to the plaintiffs. The unexplained order is a rare transgender-rights win at a court that has backed restrictions on transgender athletes and military service.
item.dc:creator: Andrew Chung, Reuters

item.title: After painting portraits of 183 fallen missionaries, Utah artist honors couple who helped make it possible
item.description: Utah artist JR Johansen, 81, who has painted 183 free portraits of Latter-day Saint missionaries who died while serving, delivered a portrait to Springville couple Cindy and Greg Thredgold based on their 1984 engagement photo. The Thredgolds, whose son Connor died of carbon monoxide poisoning on his mission in Taiwan in 2014, have since introduced other bereaved families to Johansen and backed annual gatherings for them. "My goal was that I don't want any missionary forgotten," Cindy Thredgold said.
item.dc:creator: Dan Rascon, KSL

item.title: Elizabeth Smart joins push to create 3-digit emergency number for sexual abuse survivors
item.description: Elizabeth Smart joined a WAM Safety panel at Weber State University to push for a three-digit emergency number for sexual abuse and trafficking survivors, saying "It should be like 9-1-1." A 2026 bill, HB411, which would have had state officials petition the FCC for such a hotline, stalled, and Sen. Heidi Balderree plans to sponsor a new version in 2027. Supporters argued trafficking victims may have only moments at a phone, making a short number easier to use than 10-digit lines.
item.dc:creator: Tim Vandenack, KSL

item.title: The Colorado River is shrinking. Here's why that matters for Utah's biggest cities
item.description: Part of a KSL, KUER and Salt Lake Tribune series, the story traces how the Central Utah Project, starting at Upper Stillwater Dam in Duchesne County, moves Colorado River Basin water through more than 100 miles of tunnels and pipelines to the Wasatch Front. Just over a quarter of the water used in Salt Lake, Utah and Wasatch counties comes from the basin, and the project serves 1.5 million to 2 million people. "You — living on the Wasatch Front — are the Colorado River," said Dylan Dastrup of the Central Utah Water Conservancy District, as the shrinking river raises questions for the state's largest cities.
item.dc:creator: Brooke Larsen and David Condos, The Salt Lake Tribune

item.title: Sugar House groups suddenly scrap plan for new assessment area 5 years in the making
item.description: The Sugar House Community Council and Sugar House Chamber withdrew their 2021 request for a special assessment area that would have charged businesses for economic promotion and holiday lighting, hours before the Salt Lake City Council was set to vote. City economic development director Lorena Riffo-Jenson said economic strain changed community sentiment, echoing business owners still recovering from years of road and utility construction. The entity would have overseen events and improvements in the district much as the Downtown Alliance does downtown.
item.dc:creator: Carter Williams, KSL

item.title: Provo food bank seeks $100K to keep operations afloat
item.description: Community Action Services & Food Bank in Provo, which has served the area for more than 60 years and helped over 24,000 people in the past year, says it needs $100,000 by the end of the month to keep its doors open and about $1.5 million to reach a sustainable footing. Chief impact officer Jessica Miller said community need has climbed for roughly five years while funding has tightened. Volunteer coordinator Kimber Behunin, who once relied on the food bank herself, said many people are seeking help for the first time and that "Ten dollars a month really does create a big difference."
item.dc:creator: Mike Anderson, KSL

item.title: South Korean officials free a shark trapped for a month in Busan canal
item.description: Busan officials freed Bukangi, a 9.8-foot female dusky shark that had circled a city canal for more than a month and drawn over 1.7 million visitors, on their third attempt after boats and nets failed in late September and early October. Workers on a floating platform used oars to steer the shark while crews on the banks hauled the structure about 0.6 miles toward the sea. Experts had worried about the shark, which showed no sign of feeding and faced cooling water.
item.dc:creator: Kim Tong-hyung, Associated Press

item.title: Orionid meteor shower's glowing streaks and fireballs will light up the sky
item.description: The Orionid meteor shower, produced as Earth crosses debris shed by Halley's comet, was forecast to peak at noon MDT Wednesday, making the hours after midnight into Thursday the best viewing window. A 76%-illuminated waxing gibbous moon may wash out part of the show, but it sets a few hours before sunrise, leaving a stretch when watchers could see up to 20 meteors an hour. The fast meteors, traveling about 41 miles per second, can leave lingering trains or break up into bright fireballs, and viewers are advised to get away from city light pollution.
item.dc:creator: Ashley Strickland, CNN

item.title: 'Please come forward': Partially paralyzed Utah father pleads for help finding crash witnesses
item.description: Jared Fredrickson, 33, left a C4 partial quadriplegic by a May 1 crash on state Route 59 near Hurricane during a sobriety-celebrating motorcycle ride, is asking anyone with dash cam or GoPro footage to help identify the driver responsible. The Utah Highway Patrol says a black sedan attempting an improper high-speed pass caused the multi-vehicle crash, which killed one driver, and then left the scene; six months later there are no leads. Fredrickson said the lack of accountability has also left his family without an insurance recovery as he attends therapy several times a week.
item.dc:creator: Shelby Lofton, KSL

item.title: New zoning for Smith's Ballpark redevelopment OK'd after height change
item.description: The Salt Lake City Council unanimously approved zoning for the 14.8-acre former Smith's Ballpark site, using MU-8 and MU-5 districts that allow heights up to 95 feet in some cases rather than the 150 feet possible under the MU-11 zoning first proposed. The change followed resident objections, and the city also committed to at least 5 acres of open space while protecting existing trees. Council Vice Chairwoman Erika Carlsen called the plan "largely holistic and representative" of what community members asked for.
item.dc:creator: Carter Williams, KSL

item.title: Cybersecurity firm helps educate Utah seniors about latest threats
item.description: Consultants from cybersecurity firm Arctic Wolf have spent about two years working with the Mountainland Association of Governments to teach Utah seniors current scam tactics, most recently at the Orem Public Library. Senior consultant Tanner Meeves said AI is making scams more convincing and tailored, but the core red flag remains pressure to act immediately: "there is always time." Attendees and staff described voice-phishing calls from scammers posing as a son or grandchild in trouble.
item.dc:creator: Andrew Adams, KSL

item.title: Utah State University researchers bring in a secret weapon to mitigate drought impacts
item.description: Utah State University's Beaver Ecology and Relocation group has moved about 100 nuisance beavers a year for seven years from residential areas to streams where their dams can help hold water during drought. Professor Joe Wheaton said the main storage is not the ponds but groundwater saturation across the valley that releases slowly through summer. The program quarantines beavers before release and also builds beaver dam analogs to attract them, with director Nate Norman saying "There's pretty much nothing in the ecosystem that isn't benefited by the beavers."
item.dc:creator: Paige Zamora and Mckenna Rodriguez, KSL
